## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Kandagalakajātaka* (Ja 210) is a tale in the Pali Jātaka collection, placed as the tenth story of the *Natamdaḷhavagga* [Fausböll 1879]. The opening verse begins with the words *Ambho ko nāmāyaṁ rukkho* [Fausböll 1879]. According to the narrative framework, the Buddha related this story while residing at the Veḷuvana monastery concerning Devadatta's futile efforts to imitate him (*sugātālayaṁ ārabbha*) [Fausböll 1879]. Upon hearing of Devadatta's imitation, the Buddha remarked that this was not the first time Devadatta had destroyed himself through such mimicry, and proceeded to narrate the past birth [Fausböll 1879]. The *Dhammapada-aṭṭhakathā* likewise notes that the Buddha delivered the *Kandagalaka* and *Virocana* Jātakas on successive days concerning Devadatta's self-destructive imitation [Burlingame 1921].

In the story of the past, the woodpecker Kandagalaka, accustomed to pecking at soft and rotten branches, pecked violently at a solid acacia tree (*khadira*), breaking his head and perishing on the spot [Burlingame 1921; Fausböll 1879]. In the Jātaka's resolution (*samodhāna*), the Buddha identifies Devadatta as the foolish woodpecker Kandagalaka, while the Bodhisatta was the bird Khadiravaniya [Fausböll 1879].
